title: Relative clauses in context
instructions: Choose or type the best answer. Every explanation links back to the part of the lesson that covers it.
author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)

questions.prompt: My supervisor, ___ has published widely on assessment, agreed to read my draft.
questions.explanation: This is a non-defining clause (between commas) about a person, so only *who* is possible. *That* is never used in non-defining clauses.

questions.prompt: Which sentence means that ONLY SOME of the candidates were interviewed?
options: The candidates who had relevant experience were interviewed.
The candidates, who had relevant experience, were interviewed.
questions.explanation: Without commas, the clause is defining: it picks out the candidates with experience from the others. With commas, all the candidates had experience and all were interviewed.

questions.prompt: Many lectures are now recorded, ___ allows students to review them at their own pace.
questions.explanation: The clause comments on the whole idea (that lectures are recorded), so it is a comment clause with *which*. *What* and *that* are not possible here.

questions.prompt: She's the student ___ thesis won this year's prize.
questions.explanation: *whose* + noun shows possession: the thesis belongs to the student.

questions.prompt: The survey questioned 500 teachers, most of ___ said they felt overworked.
questions.explanation: After a quantifier + *of* in a non-defining clause, use *whom* for people (*most of whom*) and *which* for things.

questions.prompt: This is the department ___ my father worked for thirty years.
questions.explanation: The clause is complete without a preposition (*my father worked there*), so use *where*. You could also say *which my father worked **in***.

questions.prompt: Formal report: ‘The conditions ___ candidates sit the exam are strictly controlled.’
questions.explanation: In formal style the preposition moves to the front, and only *which* (things) or *whom* (people) can follow it.

options: The essay which I wrote it was too long.
The essay I wrote was too long.
The essay what I wrote was too long.
questions.explanation: The relative word replaces the object, so don't repeat *it*. Because it is the object, you can also omit the relative word completely. *What* cannot follow a noun.

questions.prompt: Students ___ plagiarise their coursework are usually given a zero.
questions.explanation: The clause is the subject of *plagiarise* and refers to people, so use *who* (or *that*). *Which* is for things; *whom* is an object form.
